title: On‑Prem boot quarantine and TF drain checklist
content:
Purpose:
This note collects a compact runbook for situations where an on‑prem / VPC deployment stalls during node boot or shortly after an upgrade. It focuses on a fast quarantine flow, Terraform drain/rollout sanity checks, and a small smoke suite you can run to confirm basic runtime health.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood Private deployments (customer VPC/on‑prem installations) running the standard terraform modules from tf-modules repo.
- Assumes SSH access to at least one controller node and access to the customer’s private registry and KMS logs where applicable.
- Not an exhaustive deep dive; this is a triage checklist for the first 30–90 minutes after a failed boot/upgrade.

Quick triage summary (10–15m):
1) Isolate: mark the deployment as ‘quarantine’ in the ops dashboard and suspend autoscaler/auto‑updates to prevent further changes.
2) Snapshot: capture terraform state (terraform state pull) and upload to incident storage with timestamp.
3) Check control plane pods: kubectl get pods -A | grep -E "redwood|runtime|controller" and sort by CrashLoop/Init.
4) Collect logs: journalctl -u redwood-* --since "1 hour ago" and the last 200 lines from kubelet and containerd.
5) If boot failure: check dmesg and secure boot violations, then proceed to the detailed checks below.

Detailed checks (ordered by speed/impact):
- Network and DNS
  - Confirm node can resolve registry and internal endpoints: curl -sv https://registry.internal:443/health or dig control-plane.service.cluster.local.
  - Ensure MTU mismatch not happening (common with overlay networks): ip link show and verify mtu values align with expected (1500 or configured).
  - Check iptables/nft rules inserted by Terraform (terraform plan diff against last known good).

- System and boot diagnostics
  - dmesg | tail -n 100 -> look for file system mount errors, driver panics, GPU driver oops.
  - systemctl status kubelet containerd docker redwood-agent || journalctl -u <service> -n 200.
  - If node stuck in degraded state, check /var/log/installer.log or the distro-specific installer log for package failures.

- Container runtime and images
  - containerd/crictl: crictl ps -a; crictl images | grep redwood.
  - If image pull fails, check registry credentials (imagePullSecrets) and proxy settings on the host (HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY).
  - For air‑gapped installs, confirm the image mirror list and tgz digest match what Terraform provided.

- Certificates, KMS and identity
  - TLS errors are common after upgrades: check controller logs for x509: certificate signed by unknown authority or expired cert messages.
  - Validate KMS connectivity and key policy: kmsclient ping or look at cloud-hsm logs.
  - If cert rotation occurred in upgrade, confirm CSPs/clients trust the new CA bundle.

- Storage and mounts
  - Check mountpoints used by the runtime (kv cache, model path, docker overlay): mount | grep -E "overlay|nfs|ext4|xfs".
  - For NFS latencies: stat /path/to/model && time ls -la /path/to/model to see if list operations stall.

- GPU / driver issues (for dedicated or on‑prem GPU nodes)
  - nvidia-smi exit code and driver version: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,name --format=csv.
  - If driver mismatch after kernel update -> drain node and reinstall driver matching running kernel.

Terraform-specific notes and quick checks:
- State and drift
  - terraform state pull > state-snapshot-$(date -Iseconds).json (store in incident bucket).
  - terraform plan against the running state to detect drift; focus on network, security group, and instance metadata differences.

- Module boots and taints
  - Check for tainted resources: terraform state list | xargs -L1 terraform state show | grep -i tainted.
  - If a resource needs replacement (e.g., instance failed at cloud-init), create a safe plan to recreate with minimal blast radius: set count=1 on a single ASG/instance to test.

- Drain and rollback pattern (safe sequence):
  - 1) Mark worker nodes as unschedulable: kubectl cordon NODE; kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force (use carefully).
  - 2) Recreate or rollback the failing instance or module stage in Terraform (apply to a small subset first).
  - 3) Reboot or replace node, run smoke tests, then uncordon.
  - Note: prefer rolling back runtime+agent images rather than doing full TF rollback if the issue is binary-level.

Small smoke test suite (commands and expected results) — run from bastion or control plane:
- control-plane readiness
  - kubectl get componentstatuses -> all should be Healthy.
  - kubectl get pods -A | grep -E "redwood|runtime|model-store" -> Ready STATUS for core pods.

- end-to-end quick generation (low cost):
  - curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_API_KEY" -X POST https://internal-redwood-api/v1/generate -d '{"model":"small-debug","input":"hello"}' | jq -e '.text != null' -> exit 0 expected.
  - If API fails, capture: curl -v and capture 502/503 body for upstream error.

- KV / cache sanity
  - redis-cli -h redis.internal ping -> PONG.
  - Check prefix cache hit rate: redis-cli info | grep keyspace_hits/keyspace_misses. Sudden 0/0 often indicates misnamed keys or wrong DB index.

- Files to collect for escalation (first 20–30m):
  - /var/log/syslog, /var/log/messages (last 1k lines)
  - journalctl -u kubelet -n 500
  - journalctl -u redwood-agent -n 500
  - docker/containerd logs for failed containers (crictl logs <ctr-id>)
  - output of terraform state pull and terraform plan (redacted of secrets)

Escalation and communication checklist:
- If you hit a cryptic kernel oops, or uncertain hardware error: call SRE lead and tag on Slack #private-deployments with incident header: [QUARANTINE] <customer> <short-symptom>.
- Always attach the state snapshot and a short summary of steps taken.
- Notify PM/SE owner for the customer with ETA and whether a rollback will be attempted.

Common failure patterns seen and quick mitigations:
- Image pull auth failures after rotation: rotate imagePullSecrets to the older working secret and redeploy pod until registry rotation bug is patched.
- Kernel upgrade breaks nvidia drivers: boot into previous kernel (if available) or reprovision node with matching driver bundle.
- Terraform apply half-success (resource created but failed post-provision): mark resource with a lifecycle ignore_changes temporarily, then run post-provision script manually and capture logs.

Runbook TODOs / unresolved questions (notes to self):
- Add a small helper script to automatically gather the 10 files listed above and upload to incident S3; keep in tf-modules/tools. TODO assigned to @Diego.
- Investigate automating a safe node reprovision via terraform where only one node is replaced at a time for faster testing.
- Confirm whether we want to include kubelet --register-with-taints during upgrades to reduce scheduling.

Appendix: useful commands (copy/paste)
- snapshot TF state: terraform state pull > /tmp/state-$(date -I).json
- list recent kubelet errors: journalctl -u kubelet --since "2 hours ago" | tail -n 200
- check docker/containerd: crictl ps -a; crictl logs $(crictl ps -a -q | head -n1)
- simple API test (replace values): curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -X POST https://internal-redwood-api/v1/generate -d '{"model":"small-debug","input":"health check"}' | jq '.'

Summary:
This checklist is intentionally compact and biased toward rapid containment and evidence collection. Use it to decide whether to do a fast rollback, patch, or escalate to SRE/Platform. Keep a copy of the TF state and logs — those are critical for post‑mortem.

Notes to reviewer:
- If anything here looks risky (draining nodes blindly, terraform replacements), add an explicit pre-check and ping the on-call before doing destructive actions.
- Feedback welcome — want this to be the canonical first‑30min playbook for boot/install quiescence after upgrades.
